newsitem.title: GERMANY: German reform to cut 82 bln DM in tax - document.
newsitem.headline: German reform to cut 82 bln DM in tax - document.

text.p: The tax reform draft hammered out by Germany's coalition on Wednesday will slash 81.9 billion marks ($50 billion) in taxes but raise an extra 38.1 billion by broadening the tax base, a coalition paper showed on Thursday.
The net lightening of the tax load will come out at 43.8 billion marks as a result of measures intended to take effect in 1998 and 1999 -- the largest of which will be income tax reductions.
Still open, however, is the question of whether to raise value-added tax to help offset the cuts in direct taxation.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel, hailing the tax reform as the biggest in Germany's post-war history, said on Wednesday that Germans would be around 30 billion marks better off at the end of the day.
Key tax cuts are as follows:

-- Income tax: Incomes below 13,000 marks tax-free. Pay up to 18,000 marks taxed at 15 percent. Then, a sliding scale running from 22.5 percent comes into force, hitting a top rate of 39 percent at 90,000 marks.
-- Corporation tax: Will be cut to 35 percent on retained profits, and 25 percent on profits paid to shareholders.
-- Withholding tax: Cut to 15 percent from 25 percent.
Key measures to broaden tax base are as follows:
-- Reduction in tax exemptions on Sunday, holiday and night work.
-- Tightening up on opportunities for companies to divert funds to reserves.
-- Cutting personal travel allowance to 0.40 marks/km from 0.70 marks.
-- Halving personal interest income allowance to 3,000 marks.
